title: Finding a pawn-shop trumpet; the saxophonists who would not tune
summary: His brother got him a trumpet in Pittsburgh, and he tried to play a dance with two factory-worker brothers whose new Conn saxophones they said needed no tuning.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: When you first got to Pittsburgh, where did you get a trumpet?

I think my brother picked me one up in the pawn shop. I'm sure it had to be. He couldn't -- it wasn't new, and -- but it was a pretty good horn. And I met some guys around, and we -- give you a kind of idea what kind of musicians I was playing with. Two guys worked at the factory there, two brothers. Both of them had saxophones. One had tenor, the other had alto, and I mean they were gold instruments. Oh, they were beautiful instruments.
And we got together, and we were going to play, play

for a little dance, or something. I said, "Come on, let's tune up." He said, "I'm tuned." I said, "Well, let's get the A with the piano, there." He said, oh no, this horn -- this is a brand new Conn Karnes, this is made in tune. I don't have to tune it."

And we argued that for a good -- I said everyone tunes their horn. Oh no, see flat, you don't touch that, you know, you don't supposed to pull that out and push this in over there. This is a brand new -- and it was. It was shining like brand new gold. And don't you know, he didn't -- first I thought he was making a joke. And naturally, when we did start playing, or blowing together, you can imagine what. (Laughter.)
